item.content:encoded: La ventaja del presidente brasileño Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sobre el senador Flávio Bolsonaro se ha reducido de cara a la primera vuelta de las elecciones del domingo, según reveló el sábado una encuesta de CNT/MDA, que también apunta a una contienda más reñida en un probable balotaje. En un escenario de primera vuelta, Lula obtendría el 43,1% de los votos, seguido de Bolsonaro con el 38%. Más atrás aparecen los candidatos Augusto Cury (3,2%), Ronaldo Caiado (3%) y Renan Santos (1,5%), según el sondeo. Una encuesta del 15 de septiembre situaba a Lula en un 40,5%, a Bolsonaro en un 30,4%, a Cury en un 6%, a Caiado en un 3% y a Santos en un 2,7%. Teniendo en cuenta únicamente los votos válidos previstos, lo que excluye a quienes indicaron a la empresa encuestadora que dejarían su papeleta en blanco o la anularían de algún modo, Lula alcanzó un 47,8% de apoyo electoral frente al 42,1% de Bolsonaro. Si ningún candidato obtiene más del 50% de los votos válidos en la primera vuelta del domingo, los dos postulantes más votados pasarán a una segunda vuelta, que se celebrará el 25 de octubre. En un probable balotaje, Lula obtendría un 47,3% de apoyo electoral, frente al 43,1% del hijo mayor del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro, según la encuesta. En el sondeo anterior, Lula aventajaba al senador Bolsonaro por un 47,3% frente a un 40% en la segunda vuelta. MDA encuestó a 2.007 personas entre el 30 de septiembre y el 2 de octubre, con un margen de error del 2,2 puntos porcentuales.

item.title: Inflación de Venezuela en septiembre cierra en 8,4%: Banco Central
item.description: La inflación de Venezuela en septiembre cerró en 8,4% una leve desaceleración respecto a agosto cuando fue 8,9%, según los datos divulgados el sábado por el Banco Central.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La inflación de Venezuela en septiembre cerró en 8,4% una leve desaceleración respecto a agosto cuando fue 8,9%, según los datos divulgados el sábado por el Banco Central. Con los indicadores de septiembre, la inflación anualizada se ubicó en 465,5%, según cálculos de Reuters basados en las cifras del Banco Central (BCV). La inflación acumulada en nueve meses de este año fue 225,3%. El BCV dijo que la estabilización en el mercado cambiario incidió en el dato de septiembre. "La normalización de los flujos de ingresos externos hacia la economía nacional y el descenso de las presiones cambiarias, han motivado a que el tipo de cambio muestre un comportamiento hacia la estabilización, repercutiendo no solo en una menor brecha cambiaria, sino también en una menor variación de los precios de los bienes y servicios", agregó el comunicado.

item.title: Copiloto de flydubai atacó al piloto con un hacha en intento de "ataque terrorista", según EAU
item.description: El copiloto del vuelo FZ1073 de flydubai, con destino a Israel, intentó llevar a cabo un "ataque terrorista" con un hacha durante el vuelo, informó el sábado el fiscal general de los Emiratos Árabes Unidos.
item.dc:creator: Eman Abouhassira, Maha Dahan, Alexander Cornwell
item.content:encoded: El copiloto del vuelo FZ1073 de flydubai, con destino a Israel, intentó llevar a cabo un "ataque terrorista" con un hacha durante el vuelo, informó el sábado el fiscal general de los Emiratos Árabes Unidos. El copiloto fue identificado como Hammam al-Hammami, de nacionalidad omaní, informó a Reuters una fuente con conocimiento directo del asunto. Una segunda fuente al corriente de la investigación confirmó el nombre del copiloto. Las autoridades de los Emiratos Árabes Unidos no respondieron de inmediato a una solicitud de confirmación de su identidad. Se evitó una catástrofe el miércoles después de que los pasajeros y la tripulación redujeran al copiloto, que había atacado al capitán en lo que, según las autoridades israelíes, fue un aparente intento de estrellar el avión, en el que viajaban más de 170 pasajeros y tripulantes. Aunque las autoridades emiratíes y la aerolínea no han identificado públicamente al copiloto, funcionarios israelíes habían afirmado anteriormente que se trata de un ciudadano omaní. Omán no se ha pronunciado sobre el incidente. "Las investigaciones sobre el incidente relacionado con el vuelo FZ1073 de flydubai revelaron que el copiloto había intentado llevar a cabo un ataque terrorista", dijo el fiscal general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi en un comunicado difundido por la agencia estatal de noticias de los Emiratos Árabes Unidos. El copiloto atacó al piloto dentro de la cabina con un hacha de emergencia e intentó tomar el control de la aeronave, según el fiscal general. Normalmente, en la cabina se guarda un hacha de emergencia para su uso en situaciones de emergencia, como accidentes aéreos. La investigación sobre el vuelo FZ1073, incluidos los motivos del sospechoso, sigue en curso, y las conclusiones se darán a conocer una vez que se hayan completado los "trámites necesarios", señaló el fiscal general. Los Emiratos Árabes Unidos lideran la investigación. La aerolínea es propiedad del Gobierno de Dubái. MAYORÍA DE PASAJEROS ERAN ISRAELÍES Los comentarios del fiscal general fueron los primeros de los investigadores emiratíes en calificar el incidente como un intento de ataque terrorista. Tras la publicación de la declaración del fiscal general, Anwar Gargash, asesor principal del presidente de los EAU, dijo en X que el país del golfo tenía tolerancia cero con el terrorismo y no mostraría indulgencia alguna ante la retórica extremista. Flydubai dijo que las circunstancias que rodeaban el incidente aún se estaban investigando y que no estaba en condiciones de hacer más comentarios, dijo un portavoz el sábado. Reuters no pudo verificar de inmediato las páginas profesionales y de redes sociales que, según se informa, pertenecen al copiloto, lo que sugería que había trabajado para otras aerolíneas. Royal Air Maroc respondió a Reuters, ante una pregunta sobre su posible empleo en la compañía en el pasado, que había realizado un curso de formación de tres meses con la aerolínea en 2025, pero que su solicitud para trabajar allí posteriormente fue rechazada. RAM no dio más detalles. En sus primeras declaraciones públicas sobre el incidente, el presidente ejecutivo de flydubai, Ghaith al Ghaith, dijo el viernes que el vuelo se desvió tras un "incidente de seguridad" en la cabina de mando. La mayoría de los pasajeros a bordo eran ciudadanos israelíes. Un piloto de reserva de flydubai que viajaba en el vuelo tomó el control de la aeronave y la aterrizó en el aeropuerto de Tabuk, en el noroeste de Arabia Saudita, donde el copiloto fue detenido por las autoridades sauditas . El copiloto fue trasladado desde Arabia Saudita a Abu Dabi el jueves. Una fuente informada sobre la investigación dijo el viernes a Reuters que se esperaba que funcionarios israelíes interrogaran al copiloto en los Emiratos Árabes Unidos. La fuente se negó a precisar qué agencia o autoridad israelí participaría. Un funcionario del Gobierno israelí dijo que los investigadores israelíes participarían junto a las autoridades emiratíes en la investigación liderada por los Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Israel no mantiene relaciones diplomáticas oficiales con Omán, y el primer ministro israelí, Benjamin Netanyahu, ha declarado que no se permite a pilotos de esos países operar vuelos con destino a Israel. No estaba claro cómo el copiloto llegó a ser asignado al vuelo con destino a Tel Aviv. El viernes, Netanyahu dijo que Israel estaba investigando si el copiloto había actuado bajo las órdenes de alguien, y advirtió de que cualquier persona implicada pagaría un "alto precio". La aeronave descendió unos 16.625 pies en poco más de 30 segundos mientras sobrevolaba Arabia Saudita en su trayecto desde los Emiratos Árabes Unidos a Israel, según los datos de seguimiento de vuelos de Flightradar24. La ruta es muy popular entre los viajeros israelíes.

item.title: Lula's lead over Bolsonaro narrows ahead of Brazil vote, CNT/MDA poll shows
item.description: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's lead over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro narrowed ahead of Sunday's first-round vote, a CNT/MDA poll showed on Saturday, while also pointing to a tighter race in a likely runoff.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's lead over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro narrowed ahead of Sunday's first-round vote, a CNT/MDA poll showed on Saturday, while also pointing to a tighter race in a likely runoff. In a first-round scenario, Lula would receive 43.1% of voter support, followed by Bolsonaro (38%), Augusto Cury (3.2%), Ronaldo Caiado (3%) and Renan Santos (1.5%), according to the poll. A [USN:S0N44O037 TEXT:"September 15 poll"] had Lula at 40.5%, Bolsonaro at 30.4%, Cury at 6%, Caiado at 3% and Santos at 2.7% Considering only projected valid votes, which exclude people telling the pollster they would leave their ballots blank or void somehow, Lula reached 47.8% voter support against Bolsonaro's 42.1% If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes in the Sunday first round, the two frontrunners advance to a runoff on October 25 In a likely runoff, Lula would receive 47.3% of voter support, compared with 43.1% for the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, the poll said In the previous survey, Lula led Senator Bolsonaro by 47.3% to 40% in the runoff MDA surveyed 2,007 people from September 30 to October 2, with a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points

item.title: Lula lidera por 47,8% a 42,1% contra Flávio nos votos válidos do 1º turno, diz CNT/MDA
item.description: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está à frente do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no primeiro turno da eleição presidencial, mostrou pesquisa CNT/MDA divulgada neste sábado, véspera da eleição.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está à frente do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no primeiro turno da eleição presidencial, mostrou pesquisa CNT/MDA divulgada neste sábado, véspera da eleição. O levantamento coloca o petista com 43,1% das intenções de voto contra 38% do senador. Na pesquisa anterior, divulgada no mês passado, Lula tinha 40% e Flávio somava 30%. Os demais candidatos somados chegam agora a 9%, ante 16% na pesquisa anterior. Brancos e nulos são 5%, ante 6%, e indecisos somam 5%, ante 8%. Nos votos válidos, quando são excluídos os brancos, nulos e indecisos, Lula tem 47,8% contra 42,1% de Flávio. Na pesquisa anterior, Lula tinha 47% e Flávio somava 35%. A soma dos demais candidatos agora é de 10%, ante 18% na pesquisa anterior. Para vencer a eleição no primeiro turno, um candidato precisa ter mais de 50% dos votos válidos. Em um eventual segundo turno entre Lula e Flávio, que, se for necessário, acontecerá três semanas após a votação de domingo, no dia 25 de outubro, Lula aparece com 47,3% contra 43,1% de Flávio, o que significa um empate técnico dentro da margem de erro da pesquisa, que é de 2,2 pontos percentuais. No levantamento anterior, Lula tinha 47% e Flávio somava 40%. Brancos e nulos somam agora 8%, ante 10%, enquanto indecisos se mantiveram em 2%. Para a pesquisa, contratada pela Confederação Nacional do Transporte (CNT), o instituto MDA entrevistou 2.007 pessoas entre quarta e sexta-feira.

item.title: Fiscalía de Portugal investiga legalidad del uso de base de Lajes por parte de EEUU en la guerra de Irán
item.description: La Fiscalía portuguesa anunció el sábado que había abierto una investigación sobre la legalidad de la autorización concedida por el Gobierno de centro-derecha para que Estados Unidos utilizara la base aérea de Lajes, en las Azores, durante el conflicto con Irán, a raíz de una denuncia presentada por un partido de la oposición.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La Fiscalía portuguesa anunció el sábado que había abierto una investigación sobre la legalidad de la autorización concedida por el Gobierno de centro-derecha para que Estados Unidos utilizara la base aérea de Lajes, en las Azores, durante el conflicto con Irán, a raíz de una denuncia presentada por un partido de la oposición. Un acuerdo de larga data con Estados Unidos permite a Washington utilizar la base sin autorización previa en tiempos de paz, pero exige que Portugal dé su aprobación una vez que comiencen las hostilidades. Portugal, a diferencia de la vecina España, autorizó varios vuelos de tránsito estadounidenses a través de la base aérea de Lajes, una decisión que suscitó críticas por parte de los partidos de la oposición de izquierdas y desencadenó un debate político sobre el papel de Lisboa en las operaciones relacionadas con el conflicto con Irán. En un comunicado, la Fiscalía General dijo que "la investigación se abrió a raíz de una denuncia presentada por miembros del partido Bloque de Izquierda", sin ofrecer más detalles. El Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores de Portugal se negó a hacer comentarios. El Bloque de Izquierda solicitó en abril a la fiscalía que investigara el uso de la base de Lajes por parte de Estados Unidos, argumentando que constituía una "grave violación del derecho internacional". Sin embargo, el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, Paulo Rangel, ha afirmado que Portugal no estaba implicado en el conflicto y que el uso de la base de Lajes se ajustaba al derecho internacional, ya que se autorizó únicamente tras las garantías de Washington de que cualquier operación sería defensiva, necesaria y proporcionada, y se limitaría a objetivos militares. Los fiscales portugueses están sujetos al principio de legalidad, que les obliga a investigar presuntas irregularidades cuando existen motivos suficientes para hacerlo, a diferencia de lo que ocurre en algunas jurisdicciones, donde los fiscales disponen de una mayor discrecionalidad para decidir si un caso debe seguir adelante. La base de Lajes, situada en el archipiélago portugués de las Azores, en el Atlántico, es un centro estratégico de tránsito para las fuerzas estadounidenses en virtud de un tratado bilateral de defensa que data de 1951 y alberga la 65.ª Grupo de Base Aérea de la Fuerza Aérea de los Estados Unidos, que presta apoyo a las operaciones de Estados Unidos, la OTAN y sus aliados.

item.title: Russia pledges to continue massive strikes on Kyiv, urges foreign diplomats to leave city
item.description: The campaign is upending life for the capital's 3 million residents ahead of winter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia said on Saturday it would continue to carry out targeted retaliatory strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities and urged foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the capital. In a statement, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that "in response to the Ukrainian Armed Forces' terrorist acts against the civilian population and civilian infrastructure of our country, the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation are continuing to systematically carry out targeted strikes on military facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities". "The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs once again warns foreign nationals, including diplomatic mission staff, against staying in Ukraine or travelling to its territory. "Responsibility for any adverse consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," the ministry said. Russia has recently escalated strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital, hitting a bridge across the Dnipro river in an air attack on Saturday. The intensifying campaign has [USN:L8N44V1KC TEXT:"upended life"] for the capital's 3 million residents ahead of the bitter winter months. Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that Ukraine was paying the price for its own attacks on Russia and would continue to do so as Moscow's forces systematically strike different targets there. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on the other side's grain vessels in the Black Sea in recent months, while Russian oil refineries and other enterprises continue to come under Ukrainian shelling and Ukrainian drones kill civilians in Russian border regions. Both sides deny targeting civilians or civilian infrastructure.

item.title: US Coast Guard searches for medical aircraft carrying six from Bermuda to Boston
item.description: A medical transfer aircraft carrying six people was reported missing on a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the US Coast Guard said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Sheila Dang
item.content:encoded: A medical transfer aircraft carrying six people was reported missing on a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the US Coast Guard said on Saturday. The Federal Aviation Administration told the Coast Guard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with the plane, a Gulfstream jet, a Coast Guard spokesperson said by email. Four Canadians are on the plane, Canadian Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. "We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue," he wrote. The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12:41 a.m. local time, according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware. The plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the flight before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact, data showed. Local TV station Boston 25 posted an audio clip from Boston Logan International Airport in which an air traffic controller can be heard asking the Gulfstream pilot, "You said you're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" The controller then asked whether the plane was declaring an emergency. No response was heard. Latitude is based in Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation services. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Coast Guard said it dispatched air and surface crews to search for the plane near Nantucket, an island community south of mainland Massachusetts. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," he wrote. Weather conditions in Nantucket were clear as of Saturday afternoon, according to AccuWeather.

item.title: Portugal prosecutors probe legality of US use of Lajes base in Iran war
item.description: A longstanding agreement with the US allows it to use the Azores air base without prior authorization during peacetime.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Portuguese prosecutors said on Saturday they had opened a probe into the legality of the centre-right government's authorisation of the United States' use of the Lajes Air Base in the Azores during the Iran conflict, following a complaint by an opposition party. A longstanding agreement with the US allows Washington to use the base without prior authorisation during peacetime, but requires Portugal to give approval once hostilities begin. Portugal, unlike neighbouring Spain, [USN:L8N3ZS22H TEXT:"authorised several US transit flights"] through the Lajes air base, a decision that drew criticism from left-wing opposition parties and triggered a political debate over Lisbon's role in operations linked to the conflict with Iran. In a statement, the Prosecutor General's Office said "the probe was opened following a complaint filed by members of the Left Bloc party," without providing further details. Portugal's Foreign Ministry declined to comment. The Left Bloc asked prosecutors in April to investigate the US use of the Lajes base, arguing it amounted to a "gross violation of international law." However, Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel has said Portugal was not involved in the conflict and that the use of the Lajes base complied with international law, having been authorised only after assurances from Washington that any operation would be defensive, necessary and proportionate, and limited to military targets. Portugal's prosecutors are bound by the principle of legality, requiring them to investigate alleged wrongdoing when there are sufficient grounds to do so, unlike in some jurisdictions where prosecutors have broader discretion to decide whether a case should proceed. The Lajes base, located in Portugal's Atlantic Azores archipelago, is a strategic transit hub for US forces under a bilateral defence treaty dating back to 1951 and hosts the 65th Air Base Wing of the US Air Force, providing support for US, NATO and allied operations.

item.title: Tens of thousands protest across Spain over housing crisis
item.description: Anger swelled over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her apartment in Madrid.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night in Madrid after tens of thousands had marched across the country to demand action to tackle a housing crisis. Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, to protest the housing crisis, the Spanish government said. Earlier, some demonstrators waved posters calling for a general strike after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, and other housing issues, were [USN:L8N45F0PQ TEXT:"rejected"] in parliament on Friday. "It's a shame," said Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday's protest in Madrid. "It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can't go on like that." Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass and would be watching the strength of Saturday's protests before deciding, Spanish media reported on Friday. Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports. In the southeastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up protests. About 30 protesters entered the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural complex, before police ousted them. Other demonstrations in 50 Spanish cities were peaceful. Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told reporters in Madrid that a general strike would be called after talks with labour unions. About 70,000 protesters took part in Saturday's demonstration in Madrid, the Spanish government said. Protests planned in Barcelona and the nearby city of Hospitalet de Llobregat were called off because of heavy rain.

item.title: Indian police detain several people in Gen Z-led protests against voter roll changes
item.description: Indian police detained several people in the capital New Delhi on Saturday, disrupting a second day of protests backed by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes to voter rolls.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: Indian police detained several people in the capital New Delhi on Saturday, disrupting a second day of protests backed by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes to voter rolls. The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing party and are demanding the resignation of India's election chief. The demonstrations mark the latest in a series of youth-led protests that have emerged this year, putting pressure on Modi unprecedented in his 12 years in power. About 100 demonstrators removed security barricades on Saturday and chanted "vote thief, leave the post" and "Gyanesh Kumar, step down" before police forcibly detained some of them. Independent Member of Parliament Kapil Sibal, left-wing All India Students' Association President Neha Bora and political activists Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among the protesters, according to a Reuters witness. The police declined comment on the number and identity of those detained. "First they removed people from the voters list and now they are not letting us raise our voice against this. This is not acceptable," Bora told Reuters. The chief of the Election Commission, Kumar, has not commented on the protests and the demands to step down. On Friday, police stopped a group of protesters from gathering, bundling them into buses. Several nearby metro stations remained shut amid tight security. Though police released many of those detained on Friday, they charged several of them with allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in Delhi, according to a police source. Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls. The commission, long regarded as one of the country's most trusted institutions, says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters. On Friday the commission directed officials to register newly eligible voters and those omitted from electoral rolls.

item.title: Les Houthis revendiquent l'attaque d'un site Aramco à Ryad
item.description: Les rebelles houthis du Yémen ont annoncé avoir attaqué samedi un site d'Aramco, la compagnie pétrolière nationale de l'Arabie saoudite, situé à Ryad, capitale du royaume, avec des missiles balistiques et des drones.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les rebelles houthis du Yémen ont annoncé avoir attaqué samedi un site d'Aramco, la compagnie pétrolière nationale de l'Arabie saoudite, situé à Ryad, capitale du royaume, avec des missiles balistiques et des drones. L'Arabie saoudite n'a pas confirmé à ce stade cette information. Plus tôt dans la journée, un journaliste de Reuters a fait état d'un important panache de fumée et de flammes s'élevant à proximité d'un site de Saudi Aramco à Ryad. Aramco n'a pas répondu pour le moment à une demande de commentaires. L'incendie survient dans un contexte d'escalade des hostilités entre l'Arabie saoudite et les Houthis yéménites, proches de l'Iran, qui ont intensifié leurs attaques contre les villes et les infrastructures énergétiques saoudiennes. Les Houthis ont déclaré la semaine dernière avoir attaqué des installations d'Aramco à Yanbu à l'aide de missiles et de drones. L'Arabie saoudite avait alors dit avoir intercepté six missiles balistiques tirés par les Houthis en direction de Taïf et de la région de Yanbu, mais n'avait pas fait état de dégâts sur les installations d'Aramco.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles, drones
item.description: There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of an attack on an Aramco facility.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Saturday they had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, saying the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising in the vicinity of an Aramco facility in Riyadh earlier on Saturday, a witness told Reuters. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of an attack on an Aramco facility. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The reported attack comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure. The Houthis said last week they had attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia said at the time that it had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and the Yanbu area, but did not report damage to Aramco facilities.

item.title: Ireland coach Hallgrimsson hopes squad bonds will be stronger after tough period
item.description: Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has said his side will come out of the international window stronger after two fractious games against Israel that fans and politicians had called on his side to boycott.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has said his side will come out of the international window stronger after two fractious games against Israel that fans and politicians had [USN:L6N45I06Z TEXT:"called on his side to boycott"]. The matches had been a focus of attention since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's war in Gaza . There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel. Such was the opposition to the Irish team playing Israel that the Football Association of Ireland chose to hold the game behind closed doors in Backa Topola, a small Serbian town of around 12,000 people, rather than in Dublin. Reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who declined to be in the squad for the first game against Israel, will again be missing when the two sides meet in Serbia on Sunday, and captain Dara O’Shea will also miss out due to the birth of his child. “Football-wise, what's to come most of all is to control our focus level and keep the focus on that one (Sunday’s game against Israel), don't lose it,” the Icelandic coach told a press conference on Saturday. “There's been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well. We want to do good, but it's always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is.” TWO PROTESTS Thursday’s 2-2 draw with Austria in Dublin was briefly disrupted by two protests, but a superb goal from Troy Parrott against the Austrians and four points from their last two games have eased the pressure on the Irish team. The FAI is continuing to investigate allegations that Irish players Adam Idah and James Abankwah were racially abused in Sunday’s 3-0 win over the Israelis in Hungary. “It just goes to a process both in our departments and then to UEFA to look at,” Hallgrimsson said. “It was something that was reported from both teams. I just hope that we can focus on football and that football will be the winner after this.” The 59-year-old said the difficulties the team had faced would strengthen them. “Surviving this camp, coming out of it together as one, would be a massive win for me, that is coming from my heart,” he said. “I think all the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism, yeah, I think just surviving as a group after this game, that will be a big win for me and for this group, (and) for the (football) association.” The news conference ended abruptly when an Israeli journalist asked about an allegation that an Irish player had called an Israeli player "a monkey" during Sunday's game, with Irish press officer Kieran Crowley strongly denying the allegation before quickly bringing it to a close. Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon refused to be drawn into off-field matters. "This game is very important to us, (the) point(s) matter to come back to the group, and I'm focusing on how can I lead my team to have a good result tomorrow. This is my only focus, you can trust me on this," he told reporters. Austria top Group B3 on seven points, with Kosovo second on four ahead of the Irish on goal difference, and Israel bottom with one point.

item.title: New term gives US Supreme Court's Thomas and Alito more chances to wield power
item.description: The new US Supreme Court term that begins on Monday presents opportunities for its two eldest and most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, to help push US law further rightward on contentious issues such as gun rights, religion in public schools and voting restrictions.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: The new US Supreme Court term that begins on Monday presents opportunities for its two eldest and most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, to help push US law further rightward on contentious issues such as gun rights, religion in public schools and voting restrictions. Thomas, 78, has served on the top US judicial body since 1991, making him the [USN:L1N41E02Q TEXT:"second-longest-serving justice"] in American history. Alito, 76, has served since 2006. Earlier in their tenures, they often found themselves in dissent in major decisions, but the court, with a 6-3 conservative majority since 2020, has shifted dramatically to the right. Thomas and Alito now are perhaps at the height of their influence and have been lavished with praise by Republican President Donald Trump . 'WHY LEAVE?' If either were to retire, that would clear the way for Trump to nominate a younger conservative replacement who could serve for decades in the lifetime position. But, at least for now, according to legal experts, they appear more interested in wielding that power than stepping aside. "They have been waiting for a long time to be in the position," political science professor Kevin McMahon of Trinity College in Connecticut said of Thomas and Alito. "So why leave?" During the court's term that ended in June, Thomas and Alito helped deliver long-sought victories to the conservative legal movement. These included a [USN:S0N3YR013 TEXT:"ruling"] expanding presidential control over regulatory agencies, and a [USN:S0N3YR00L TEXT:"decision"] further limiting the scope of the Voting Rights Act, the landmark 1965 law intended to eliminate racial discrimination in voting. Thomas and Alito have been Trump's most reliable votes in cases involving his extraordinary exertion of presidential powers. [USN:L1N45H0WL TEXT:"More such cases are coming"] during the new nine-month term, including two involving Trump's hardline [USN:S0N43101E TEXT:"immigration policies"]. The court's docket also includes November 3 arguments in a [USN:L1N4130K0 TEXT:"challenge"] to a Colorado law requiring preschools receiving taxpayer money to enroll children of same-sex couples, the latest clash between religious rights and LGBT protections to reach the justices. The justices also may take up a case examining whether a Texas law that requires public elementary and high schools to display the [USN:L1N45G0IM TEXT:"biblical Ten Commandments"] in classrooms comports with the US Constitution's prohibition on the government establishing or endorsing any particular religion or promoting religion over nonreligion. On December 2, the court will [USN:S0N3YR01V TEXT:"hear"] arguments over whether states can ban AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles, an opportunity for the conservative justices to further expand gun rights. Thomas and Alito have been instrumental in major guns rulings since 2008. On December 8, the court will [USN:S0N41Y01G TEXT:"consider"] whether Arizona can mandate that people registering to vote provide proof of citizenship, a Republican-backed measure critics have called an effort to make it harder for groups who tend to support Democratic candidates to register. Legal experts said these cases give Thomas and Alito chances to build on some of their most influential earlier rulings and target more Supreme Court precedents they consider misguided. "They have more they want to accomplish, and I expect them to keep pushing on a host of issues," McMahon said, adding that they even may envision themselves serving as a check on a potential future Democratic president beginning in 2029. "They're still in their seventies," McMahon said. "And for a Supreme Court justice, it's not unprecedented that you stay on the bench well into your eighties." 'LEGENDS, BOTH' Thomas and Alito backed every major Trump administration policy that came before the court last term, unlike the three conservative justices Trump appointed during his first term — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. Those three all have compiled very conservative records as justices but in a few major cases sided against Trump. Trump [USN:L6N45N0QS TEXT:"told"] Time magazine this week he regretted nominating all three, calling them disloyal. "I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often," Trump said. Thomas and Alito, on the other hand, are "[USN:FWN4570D3 TEXT:"legends, both"]," Trump said last month after they dissented from a decision that blocked his plans to restrict mail-in voting. "Alito and Thomas are the two who have figured out how to never get into Trump's doghouse," University of Minnesota political science professor Timothy Johnson said. Alito rejected the notion that he is a rubber stamp for Trump and his administration, telling the Wall Street Journal in August: "I vote in every case the way I think the case should be decided. If that means a high correlation with what Trump wants, fine. If it means zero correlation with what Trump wants, fine as well." 'A VALUABLE CONTRIBUTION' Speculation among court watchers about a possible vacancy has ramped up as the two men draw closer to the average age of retirement for Supreme Court justices since 2000 — about 80 years old — and with the November 3 US congressional elections looming. If Democrats take control of the Senate, they could try to block Trump's nominee to fill any vacancy created by the retirement or death of a sitting justice. Alito tamped down retirement speculation for now, telling the Wall Street Journal: "Obviously, I'm here for another term." The term runs through the end of June. In a CBS News interview excerpt released on Friday, Alito said he thought about retiring this year, calling retirement something someone his age must think about every year. "But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place," Alito said. "It's too hard to predict, for anybody, particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now, and so forth," Alito said. "And it's too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement." ABORTION RIGHTS Alito has a lot of influence in conversations among the court's conservatives, said Peter Canellos, author of a recent Alito biography titled "Revenge for the Sixties." "A lot of the action on the Supreme Court right now is conservative on conservative," Canellos said. "It's entirely a discussion among conservatives." Canellos said Alito's influence was highlighted by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, perhaps the most important ruling he has authored. It overturned the 1973 Roe v. Wade precedent that had recognized a woman's constitutional right to have an abortion. Chief Justice John Roberts, a stalwart conservative, dissented from the portion of Alito's ruling that reversed Roe. "I think over the years Alito has thought of himself as an instrumental justice," Canellos said. "You can see in many cases, Dobbs included, that his key ability is to bring the three Trump appointees to his side, rather than Chief Justice Roberts' side, when the two of them disagree." In Dobbs, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett joined Alito. "I suspect that Alito felt that even if he were replaced by a true conservative, which was the core of the argument why he should resign, it was not in any way preordained that that person would have the kind of influence that he has," Canellos added. Alito has long criticized a 1990 Supreme Court precedent that limits the ability of people to seek religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Religious rights advocates have said that ruling infringes on First Amendment protections for free exercise of religion. The 1990 ruling specifically held that the First Amendment does not protect people who participate in illegal acts — in that case, the use of an illegal hallucinogenic drug — as part of a religious ceremony. The religious freedom case being argued in November, called St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, gives Alito and the other conservative justices a chance to cast doubt on the 1990 precedent, known as Employment Division v. Smith. 'WHY NOT CONTINUE?' The case involving state-level bans on assault-style rifles may give Thomas a chance to clarify a test he laid out in one of his most impactful rulings, a 2022 case called New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Under this test, gun control measures must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" — not simply advance an important government interest — in order to comply with the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms. Some judges have said this wording does not provide clear guidance, producing inconsistent results. "He has clearly expressed frustration that his colleagues have dodged reviews of assault-weapon prohibitions, making these consolidated challenges from Connecticut and Illinois a long-sought vehicle to establish a nationwide constitutional rule that includes these specific guns," Johnson said of Thomas. Thomas has not addressed retirement rumors, but in the past has hinted at a lengthy tenure. McMahon said Thomas may want to become the longest-serving justice, a milestone he would reach in May 2028. "If you're that close, and you have the setup that he has, why not continue?" McMahon asked.

item.title: India, Pakistan summon top diplomats over border incident
item.description: India and Pakistan summoned each other's top diplomats on Saturday over a border incident on October 2, with New Delhi rejecting Islamabad's allegation that Indian forces had killed two unarmed Pakistani civilians and saying those involved had crossed illegally into Indian territory.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India and Pakistan summoned each other's top diplomats on Saturday over a border incident on October 2, with New Delhi rejecting Islamabad's allegation that Indian forces had killed two unarmed Pakistani civilians and saying those involved had crossed illegally into Indian territory. Pakistan's foreign ministry said earlier on Saturday that personnel from India's Border Security Force had used "unprovoked lethal force" against two unarmed Pakistani civilians in the Bedian sector along the international border on Friday. "Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterize the deceased as 'infiltrators'," the ministry said in a statement. Pakistan said it had summoned India's chargé d'affaires to lodge a protest over the incident and called for an "immediate, transparent and credible investigation". India's foreign ministry later rejected what it called "baseless and motivated allegations" and said it had summoned the chargé d'affaires of the Pakistan High Commission to protest at the "continued facilitation of illegal cross-border infiltration from Pakistan". The ministry said three people had crossed into Indian territory in the Ferozepur sector of Punjab and continued moving towards the border fence despite multiple warnings from the BSF to return to Pakistan. "The BSF was compelled to engage them for posing an imminent security threat," the ministry said. India said the incident reflected "a clear pattern of repeated cross-border movement by armed narcotics syndicates operating from Pakistan" and urged Islamabad to investigate what it described as cross-border infiltration and drug-smuggling activities. India also urged Pakistan to respect the international border, observe bilateral arrangements and ensure its forces prevented unauthorised movement from its side. Relations between the two nuclear-armed rivals have been strained since a four-day war in 2025, the worst in decades, followed by a militant attack on tourists in Indian Kashmir that killed 26 people. New Delhi accused Pakistan of backing the attack, which Islamabad denied.

item.title: Ethiopia government forces retake airport in Tigray's capital, sources say
item.description: Ethiopia's federal military has recaptured the main airport in the capital of the northern Tigray region, three sources said on Saturday, dealing a major setback to an opposition alliance in its stronghold.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ethiopia's federal military has recaptured the main airport in the capital of the northern Tigray region, three sources said on Saturday, dealing a major setback to an opposition alliance in its stronghold. Clashes pitting a rebel alliance led by Tigray's ruling party against the government and its allied forces [USN:L6N45G0U0 TEXT:"broke out"] in northern Ethiopia last week, in the most serious escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war. The fighting has stoked fears that it could escalate into a [USN:L6N45M0WY TEXT:"wider regional conflict"], potentially drawing in neighbouring countries in the Horn of Africa and the Gulf. In Washington, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the United States strongly urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to "exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation as agreed in their 2018 peace framework." "The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis," Pigott said. "A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries." The federal government in Addis Ababa severed diplomatic ties with Eritrea this week, accusing it of supporting the rebel alliance alongside Sudan and Egypt. The three countries deny this. Troops from the Ethiopian National Defence Forces had regained control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Tigray's capital Mekelle, one source with knowledge of events in the city and a humanitarian source told Reuters. A third source, a Mekelle resident who asked not to be named for security reasons, confirmed the taking of the airport by government forces and added they could hear gunfire outside the city centre. This source said they had seen some Tigrayan Defence Force fighters abandoning their posts and heading home, and that there was looting of government facilities taking place in the city. Reuters could not immediately verify the assertions and the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), could not be immediately reached for comment. A source close to the TPLF however told Reuters the city was encircled by government troops and allied militias. Mekelle's airport, which is around 10 km (6 miles) from the centre of the city, was one of three airports in the region that were [USN:L6N45G0U0 TEXT:"seized"] by the opposition forces at the start of the fighting on September 23. The taking of Mekelle by government forces would be a major setback for the opposition alliance, although analysts say it would be unlikely to end the conflict. In 2020, federal forces captured Mekelle within the first month of the two year war before the TPLF reclaimed it seven months later.

item.title: High school students in Paris' deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
item.description: More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head.
item.dc:creator: Layli Foroudi
item.content:encoded: Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in [USN:L1N45O03R TEXT:"protests"] that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages. At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighborhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions. “Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,” Maisa said. "These are not conditions to study in." As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a "climate of unacceptable violence" and called for order. Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading, "Our address should not decide our future". She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country. "The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It's classist and racist," she said. Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France's marginalised urban neighbourhoods are increasingly influencing national politics. "When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at bottom," he said. POLITICAL FLASHPOINT The nationwide demonstrations and blockades, which[USN:L6N45M0ED TEXT:" began last week"], have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular[USN:L8N4590SH TEXT:" spending cuts"] in its 2027 budget on Thursday. The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7% to €65.53 billion, excluding teacher pensions. The education ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline. The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille. At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been canceled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative. In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Thursday, the CGT labour union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages including of nurses and social workers. Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT's education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs. Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey. NOT ENOUGH TEACHERS "Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don't have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments," she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026. In Pantin, a town on the northeastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police. "What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers — which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity," she said. While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at €11,660 in 2024 and €11,910 in 2010, according to education ministry data. The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalauréat, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Professor Clemence Cardon-Quint at Paul Valery University, who researches education funding. The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools. Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticised by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory. "In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Cardon-Quint.

item.title: Latvian PM Kulbergs strongly ahead in election, according to exit poll
item.description: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party was seen winning a parliamentary election on Saturday by an unexpectedly wide margin, exit polls showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas, Terje Solsvik
item.content:encoded: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party was seen winning a parliamentary election on Saturday by an unexpectedly wide margin, exit polls showed, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression. An exit poll by Latvian public broadcaster LSM showed United List winning 35.6% of votes, followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First at 11.3%. Latvia First had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber- and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although Western officials dismiss concerns it is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO, of which Latvia is a member. Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Reacting to the exit poll reading, Kulbergs said he hoped to remain prime minister, but said he would not want to govern with Latvia First. If exit polls were confirmed by official results, he would still need coalition allies to form a government. "It's remarkably good. I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga. Third in the exit poll ranking was the Progressives party, on 11.3%, followed by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power with 10.8%. SHADOW OF UKRAINE WAR A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which [USN:L1N41K03T TEXT:"stray military drones flew"] undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"have blamed Russia"] for causing them to divert from their flight paths. Throughout his campaign, he has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. But his pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority. "Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts," Sovereign Power party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. "The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks." The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin's war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, and Russia and Belarus to the east.

item.title: Israeli strike kills five in Gaza, including four women, health officials say
item.description: An Israeli airstrike killed at least five Palestinians, including four women, in an apartment building in Gaza City early on Saturday, health and civil defence service officials said.
item.dc:creator: Nidal Al-Mughrabi, Dawoud Abu Alkas
item.content:encoded: An Israeli airstrike killed at least five Palestinians, including four women, in an apartment building in Gaza City early on Saturday, health and civil defence service officials said. Among the dead were a Christian mother, Maisa Abu Dawoud, and her daughter Mary, medics and the church said. The Israeli military said later on Saturday that it carried out an overnight strike on an apartment in Gaza in an attempt to kill Ali al-Amoudi. Hamas sources said al-Amoudi leads the Hamas political office in Gaza. It was not immediately clear whether that was the same strike that killed the five Palestinians. The military said the results of the strike were under review, while Hamas did not immediately comment. The strike that killed the five Palestinians destroyed the apartment building and started a fire. "We were asleep and suddenly heard continuous strikes and heavy explosions. The children woke up startled and started running and screaming," said witness Ahmed al-Dahdouh. "We ran out and found that our neighbour's house was struck and there were dismembered martyrs, women, men and children. We started to pull them out; they were scattered under the rubble," he told Reuters. Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of the ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. FUNERAL IN GAZA CITY Friends, including Muslims, and relatives gathered at the Saint Porphyrius Church in Gaza City to pay their respects during the funeral of the Christian mother and daughter. Christians make up just 1% of Gaza's more than 2 million population. "Today is essentially the worst day of my life. I lost my mother and my grandmother today," said Fouad al-Najjar. In a statement later on Saturday, the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem mourned Maisa Abu Dawoud and her daughter, Mary, extending condolences to their family. "We pray for an end to the war and bombardment, for the protection of civilian lives, and for a just peace in which the people of Gaza can feel secure for their children and loved ones. May their memory be eternal,” the Patriarchate said. Gaza health officials have said at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since last October's ceasefire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period.

item.title: What do we know about flydubai flight 1073?
item.description: Here is what we know, and don't know.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Here is what we know, and don't know, about the reported attempt by the copilot of flydubai flight 1073 to crash the plane on September 30 before it landed safely in Saudi Arabia. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE PLANE? The flight, carrying more than 170 mostly Israeli passengers and crew, departed Dubai at 0305 GMT, according to flight data reviewed by Reuters. At 0521 GMT in Saudi airspace it made a sudden, sharp turn and plunged towards the ground twice, before stabilising. The plane fell more than 16,000 feet in just over 30 seconds during its most dramatic dive. It then put out distress signals indicating an emergency and unlawful interference. It changed course over Jordanian airspace and diverted to land in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. At one point the transponder was turned off for nearly half an hour, according to an Israeli official. WHAT HAPPENED IN THE COCKPIT? The copilot attacked and wounded the captain during the flight, the captain, Israeli and Saudi officials say. The copilot [USN:L1N45P01E TEXT:"used an axe"], which is normally kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies, for the attack, the United Arab Emirates' prosecutor general said. During one of the plane's plunges, [USN:L1N45O05O TEXT:"the wounded captain"] who was lying on the floor managed to open the door, he said, allowing passengers to enter the cockpit and overpower the copilot. Israeli officials cite witnesses saying that the copilot was "bashing" the control panel, without elaborating. They say the copilot appeared to be trying to crash the plane. [USN:L8N45N0K6 TEXT:"One of the passengers"] managed to steady the plane after the copilot was subdued, which he knew how to do after watching an air-crash TV show, according to his own account. A second pair of off-duty pilots on board then took the controls and landed, according to witnesses and Israeli officials. Both the copilot and the captain suffered injuries, Saudi officials said. Videos from inside the cabin verified by Reuters show a wounded captain and copilot and blood apparently smeared on walls, and the copilot restrained by the passengers. WHAT ISN'T CLEAR? The UAE's prosecutor general is calling the copilot's actions an attempted "terrorist attack". It has not said what that attack might have entailed if successful, and what the motivations were. We also don't know the exact timings of events on board, such as at what time the copilot overpowered the captain. There was initial speculation the copilot had a knife because a passenger on board asked about a knife in one video of the incident. There has been no further information on that. HOW CLOSE DID THE PLANE COME TO CRASHING? At its steepest point, the plane was losing altitude at about 544 feet (166 metres) per second. Similar trajectories have resulted in several major crashes. WHAT ROLE DID PASSENGERS PLAY? One woman noticed a commotion in the cockpit when the captain opened the door and alerted the rest of the plane. At least four [USN:L6N45M12C TEXT:"passengers rushed towards the cockpit"], attacking and restraining the copilot. The passenger who then steadied the plane before the off-duty pilots could take over said he first pulled the copilot away from the controls with the help of the other passengers. Two other passengers attacked the copilot and tied him up using earphone cables, one of them said. A doctor on board treated the wounded captain. WHY WERE THERE OTHER TRAINED PILOTS ON THE FLIGHT? The two off-duty flydubai pilots were likely on board as backup for tired crew, a pilot interviewed by Reuters said. Middle East flights often have to reroute because of the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, the pilot said. [USN:L4N45N0NH TEXT:"Flydubai"] said on Friday a full investigation was underway. WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE COPILOT? The copilot's identity has not been publicly confirmed. But two sources with knowledge of the incident have told Reuters he has been identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Israeli officials say he is Omani. Omani authorities have not commented and there has been no comment from him or a representative. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu [USN:L1N45N0GR TEXT:"told Fox News"] that the copilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination", without providing details, and that he was suicidal. Israeli security officials have said he was likely acting alone, though the investigation is ongoing. Israel's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates has said no motive has been determined. The copilot had trained with Royal Air Maroc, but RAM said it rejected his application to work there. WAS IRAN OR ANOTHER COUNTRY INVOLVED? Israeli security officials say Israel had not identified any Iranian involvement so far. Iran has not commented. WHO IS HANDLING THE INVESTIGATION? The United Arab Emirates has [USN:S8N43T02X TEXT:"ordered"] an investigation. UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag. Netanyahu said Israel, which has a close diplomatic and security relationship with the UAE, will be "possibly participating" in the investigation. Saudi Arabia said it had conducted the preliminary investigation with security teams from the UAE. HOW WAS THIS ALLOWED TO HAPPEN? Pilots undergo background checks and regular psychological assessments, part of stringent measures in place since the 9/11 attacks in the United States in 2001. Israel has strict screening for anyone travelling there. That includes not normally allowing in pilots from countries without diplomatic relationships with Israel, such as Oman. Netanyahu has said Israel will look at the "loophole" that allowed the copilot on board. Israel is set to [USN:S8N45108C TEXT:"ramp up"] security checks on pilots flying into the country, Netanyahu's office said.

item.title: Israeli officials to question co-pilot of flydubai flight, source says
item.description: Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial passenger flight from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Cornwell
item.content:encoded: Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial [USN:L6N45N0GW TEXT:"passenger flight"] from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation. Disaster was averted on [USN:L4N45N0NH TEXT:"flydubai"] flight FZ1073 on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had [USN:L1N45M07P TEXT:"stabbed"] the captain in what Israeli officials have said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying over 170 passengers and crew. A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the flight landed the plane at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi Arabian authorities. The co-pilot was transferred on Thursday to the UAE, where the source said Israeli officials were expected to question him. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part in the questioning. Asked whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot, an Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background. The UAE foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot. In his first public comments on the incident, flydubai Chief Executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said on Friday that authorities were conducting an official investigation, supported by the airline, after what he described as a "safety incident" in the cockpit. "It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts," he said in a written statement, acknowledging that there were "many questions" about what happened on flight FZ1073. The UAE state news agency reported on Thursday that Emirati authorities had opened an investigation seeking to establish the circumstances and motives and determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction". MOTIVE NOT YET ESTABLISHED Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning in a video statement released by his office that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price". Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals. Netanyahu on Thursday said that the co-pilot, whom he has identified as an Omani national, had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, but that so far a motive for his actions had not been established. Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has said pilots from such countries were not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It was not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv. The aircraft plunged some 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds as it flew over Saudi Arabia on the journey from the United Arab Emirates to Israel, according to data from flight tracker Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israelis. CAPTAIN HAILED AS HERO The co-pilot's identity has not been publicly disclosed beyond his nationality. The captain who was stabbed has been identified as Indian national [USN:L4N45M1MF TEXT:"Smit Machchhar"], who has been [USN:L1N45N01H TEXT:"hailed"] as a hero by Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Omani authorities have not commented on the incident. The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote on October 27, in the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, with Israel's security featuring prominently in the campaigning. The US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, in a war that quickly spread to the Gulf and Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah. Since coming under attack by Iran this year, the UAE has strengthened its relationships with Israel, with which it opened ties as a result of the 2020 Abraham Accords.

item.title: A remarkable Q3, French woes and Trump's diesel hit: The financial week in five charts
item.description: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days.
item.dc:creator: Anna Szymanski
item.content:encoded: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest (ROI) distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days. 1. TALE OF TWO QUARTERS JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: Wednesday capped an extraordinary quarter marked by a bond rout that sent [USN:L1N45K0MU TEXT:"yields"] to multi-decade-highs around the world, a 40% jump in Brent crude and [USN:L1N45G0Q3 TEXT:"record-high diesel prices."] Yet US and global stocks still scaled fresh record highs, driven by eye-popping corporate earnings growth. While equity gains were modest, they were still notable given the dismal backdrop and the fact that they were coming off the strongest three-month period in six years. As the final quarter of 2026 begins, the question is whether stocks can [USN:L6N45N036 TEXT:"continue to grind higher"] even as global bond woes continue. 2. PAS BIEN ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: While the bond rout has hit most developed markets, France stands out — for the wrong reasons. The country's 10-year borrowing cost surged to its highest level since 2002 on Thursday, nearing the psychologically important 5% mark following its worst quarterly performance since 1987. This helped widen the gap between French and German 10-year borrowing costs, which is currently close to the broadest it has been since the euro zone debt crisis. The cost of insuring France's debt against the risk of default has also leapt to its highest point since 2013. This comes as the government is putting forward a 2027 budget bill that could struggle to get through parliament given its [USN:L1N45N09R TEXT:"unpopular belt-tightening measures"]. French public sector workers held a strike on Tuesday over a proposed wage freeze, while [USN:L6N45M0ED TEXT:"students' demonstrations"] over a lack of resources for schools have turned increasingly violent. 3. DIESEL'S POLITICAL TOLL GAVIN MAGUIRE, ROI Global Energy Transition Columnist: The Trump administration has told Germany and France to [USN:L6N45N0FO TEXT:"draw down their emergency diesel inventories"] to help ease the global fuel squeeze or face a potential US diesel export ban. Diesel prices remain near record highs, which is hitting the trucking and farming sectors hard. This appears to be weighing on US President Donald [USN:L6N45D0NV TEXT:"Trump's approval ratings"] and could be helping to drive a broad shift toward Democrats ahead of November's midterm elections. (The potential relationship between diesel prices and the likelihood of Democrats winning control of the Senate was initially indicated by Barclays.) 4. OCTOBER DOUBTS MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: The past 10 days have seen sharp swings in market expectations for the October Federal Reserve meeting. Incoming economic data and policymakers' speeches initially pushed futures-market-implied odds of a rate hike to 70%. But those odds retreated to around, or below, 50% after New York Federal Reserve President John Williams this week [USN:S0N44U01W TEXT:"steered clear"] of endorsing consecutive rate increases. 5. AN EXISTENTIAL INVESTMENT? ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: Anthropic plans a mammoth investment of more than half a trillion dollars in computing infrastructure over the coming years, according to its confidential IPO prospectus, [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"which Reuters saw earlier this week"]. But the AI startup lab, which is targeting a $2 trillion valuation, [USN:L4N45K1J5 TEXT:"also reiterated warnings"] that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." That's an interesting position for both Anthropic and its investors. Is plowing more money into AI a way to shore up the technology's promise and avert its peril? [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:"Or is it simply perilous?"] Opinions expressed are those of the authors. They do not reflect the views of Reuters News, which, under the Trust Principles , is committed to integrity, independence, and freedom from bias.

item.title: Man City appeal Premier League financial ruling
item.description: The league said City used sham commercial contracts to inflate revenue and understate costs.
item.dc:creator: Lori Ewing
item.content:encoded: Manchester City have filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid [USN:L6N45K0U6 TEXT:"potentially severe sanctions."] The league said on Tuesday that City had used [USN:L6N45L10S TEXT:""sham" commercial contracts"] as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.19 billion) over nearly a decade. City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation. The club, who had until the end of the day on Friday to appeal, has denied wrongdoing throughout the process. With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league. "Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," the club said in a statement. "The Club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. "The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case." The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member board appointed by the chair of the league’s judicial panel. "The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the Judicial Panel," the league said in a statement. "The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted." The Premier League's new fast-track rules state that an appeal hearing should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding. Some legal commentators expect City to argue that those rules did not exist when the club were originally charged in February 2023. APPEAL HELD IN PRIVATE The appeal will take place in private, as did the original hearings. The board will review the commission's decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case. The board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or compensation order imposed. A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit a subsequent arbitration process. City can also separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard, and whether they would take effect immediately. A league representative told Reuters they could not discuss the process for [USN:L1N45M0DF TEXT:"confidentiality reasons."] While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11. WIDER REPERCUSSIONS In its first public statement since the commission's findings were announced, the Football Association said on Friday it was closely monitoring the case. "The Independent Commission's decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game," the FA said in a statement. "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate." The repercussions facing City could extend beyond football. On Thursday, the chair of parliament's Treasury Committee [USN:L6N45L10G TEXT:"Meg Hillier"] asked Britain's tax authority HMRC what action it was taking in response to the commission's findings. Hillier said she had written to HMRC Permanent Secretary JP Marks following the publication on Tuesday of the independent commission ruling that the club had committed "well over 100 individual breaches of the Premier League Rules across the course of many seasons". Some sports lawyers have predicted [USN:L4N45M0A3 TEXT:"years"] of further litigation as rival clubs, players and agents assess whether they may have grounds to pursue compensation claims connected to the case. ($1 = 0.7572 pounds)

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Spiking bond yields, midterms, earnings to test US stocks' typical fourth-quarter strength
item.description: Bond yields, the midterms and earnings likely will test US stocks' typical fourth-quarter strength.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: Investors head into a part of the calendar that tends to be upbeat for US stocks, but that seasonal strength is under threat from a number of challenges, including a surge in bond yields and the market's apparent dependence on massive AI spending. As the fourth quarter kicks off, the stock market is already on pace for a solid year. The benchmark S&P 500 (.SPX) as of Friday had gained nearly 13% in 2026, and sat about 1% below its mid-August record high. Markets face a busy end of 2026, with the start of corporate earnings season and a pivotal Federal Reserve meeting in coming weeks, along with the looming November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress. "It does tend to be a seasonally strong period, however I think this year investors are facing some headwinds as we go into the fourth quarter," said Tracie McMillion, head of global asset allocation strategy at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Q4 TENDS TO SEE STOCK GAINS Since 1945, the S&P 500 averaged an increase of 4.2% in the fourth quarter, with the index posting gains 85% of the time, according to research firm CFRA. That average percentage rise is more than twice that of the other three quarters. Fourth quarters of midterm years have generally been even stronger, with an average gain of 6.4%, as stocks "benefit from the lifting of election uncertainty," Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA, said in a note. While fourth quarters tend to shine, mid-term years overall historically have been subpar, a trend stocks have defied so far in 2026. The S&P 500 has averaged a 15% dip in midterm years historically, while the deepest drop so far this year has only been 9%, according to McMillion of the Wells Fargo institute.
